title: Linked lists: nodes, traversal, insertion and deletion
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion update links; dynamically allocated nodes require explicit ownership and release.
understand.whyItMatters: Linked lists allow insertion and removal without shifting an array, but traversal is sequential and pointer mistakes can lose nodes or access freed storage.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion update links; dynamically allocated nodes require explicit ownership and release.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function receives a pointer to the head pointer so it can update the caller's list head. A new node points to the old head before the head is replaced.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the pointer changes when inserting before the first node.
practise.independentTask: Implement traversal, search, deletion and full-list cleanup, including deletion of the head node.
hints: Update links before freeing a node that is being removed.
Check allocation failure before dereferencing the new node.
Define who owns the list and who is responsible for freeing all nodes.
